docs.title: Materials overview
docs.text:
This section concisely describes the mechanical models implemented in Comfor. For a more detailed introduction, the reader is recommended to refer to the following links, as well as to consult the cited papers.

  • Nonlinear continuum mechanics
  • Composite material introduction

docs.title: Comfor constitutive models
docs.text:
Comfor includes the following constitutive models.

  • Elasticity
    • Kirchhoff isotropic
  • Hyper-elasticity
    • Ogden
    • Textile elasticity

The following parameter must be set for all the materials:

Necessary parameters

  • material_name is the custom name for the material
  • \(\rho\) the mass density of the material.

Optional parameters

  • \(\alpha\) is the mass proportional damping. This factor introduces damping forces caused by the absolute velocities of the model. This parameter is optional.

Example

MATERIALS TYPE <material_type_1>
<material_name> RHO = <mass density> DAMPING = <damping_value> ...

docs.title: Elastic materials
docs.text:
In order to model elastic materials with small strain are large rotations we use a Saint-Venant-Kirchoff material model. The general expression is given by:

\[ \mathbf{S} = \mathbb{C} \mathbf{E} \]

where \(\mathbb{C}\) elastic tensor or elastic moduli.

docs.title: Isotropic Kirchhoff
docs.text:
In tha case of an isotropic material the elastic moduli is given simply by :

\[ \mathbb{C} = \lambda \mathbf{I} \otimes \mathbf{I} + 2\mu \mathbf{I} \]

where \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\) are the Lamé constants related to the \(E\) Young's modulus and \( u\) Poisson's ratio.

\[ egin{aligned} \lambda &= rac{ u E}{\left( 1 + u ight)\left( 1 - 2 u ight)} \ \mu &= rac{E}{2\left( 1 + u ight)} \end{aligned} \]

The stress-strain relation is given simply by:

\[ \mathbf{S} = \mathbb{C}:\mathbf{E} \]

Expected parameters

  • \(E\) : Young's modulus
  • \( u\) : Poisson's ratio.

Example

MATERIALS TYPE ELASTIC
<material_name> RHO = <rho> DAMPING = <material_damping> E = <young_modulus> NU = <poissons_ratio>

docs.title: Hyperelastic materials
docs.text:
Two families of hyperelastic materials are currently implemented:

  • Isotropic to model vacuum bags, rubbery like membrane materials ...
  • Anisotropic textiles models.

The general form for the strain-stress relation is given by:

\[ \mathbf{S} = 2 \frac{\partial w}{\partial \mathbf{C}} \]

where \(w\) is the strain-energy potential of the material.

docs.title: Isotropic hyperelastic materials
docs.text:
Ogden

The strain energy potential for this constitutive model is defined by a polynomial series as a function of the principal stretches.

\[ w \left( \lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3 \right) = \sum_{p=1}^N \frac{\mu_p}{\alpha_p} \left( \lambda_1^{\alpha_p}+ \lambda_2^{\alpha_p} + \lambda_3^{\alpha_p} - 3 \right) \]

Where N is a positive integer generally taken equal to 3, and \(\mu_p\) and \(\alpha_p\) are the material parameters to be identified. In the case of hyperelastic membranes, an assumption of incompressibility is generally made. The conservation of volume can be expressed in terms of the principal elongations:

\[ \lambda_1 \lambda_2 \lambda_3 = 1 \]

This allows us to express the thickness evolution as a function of the membrane strains:

\[ \lambda_3 = \frac{1}{\lambda_1 \lambda_2} = \frac{h}{h_0} \]

Finally, the stress state expressed in the initial configuration under the assumption of an incompressible material is given by:

\[ \mathbf{S} = 2 \frac{\partial w \left( \lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3 \right) }{\partial \mathbf{C}} - p\mathbf{C}^{-1} \]

With p being the Lagrange multiplier associated with the incompressibility condition of the material (hydrostatic pressure).

Expected parameters

  • TYPE : OGDEN
  • \(\mu_i\) : shear moduli constant values.
  • \(\alpha_i\) : constant dimensionless values associated to each \(\mu_i\).

Example

MATERIALS TYPE HYPERELASTIC
<material_name> RHO = <rho> DAMPING = <material_damping> TYPE = OGDEN MU = <mu_1 mu_2 mu_3 mu_n> ALPHA = <alpha_1 alpha_2 alpha_3 alpha_n>

Note

  • \(N\) is deduced automatically from the number of parameters given in the material entry.
  • The initial thickness \(h_0\) is deduced from the element definition

Warning

The number of \(\mu_p\) and \(\alpha_p\) parameters must be equal.

docs.title: Textile composite hyperelastic materials
docs.text:
The mechanical behavior of textile composite materials can modelled using a non-linear hyperelastic model1 2. The membrane and bending contributions to the strain energy potential are decoupled given the fibrous nature of one single ply.

\[ w = {w_{mem}} + {w_{ben}} \]

The membrane strain energy is expressed as a function of the physical invariants associated with the different deformation modes of the reinforcement.

\[ \begin{equation} w_{mem}\left( I_{\lambda_1} ,I_{\lambda_2} ,I_{\gamma} \right) = w_{\lambda_1}\left( I_{\lambda_1}\right) + w_{\lambda_2}\left(I_{\lambda_2}\right) + w_{\gamma}\left(I_{\gamma}\right) \end{equation} \]

with:

\[ \begin{aligned} I_{\lambda_1} & = \frac{1}{2}\ln\left( I_{41} \right) = \ln \left( {\lambda_1} \right) \\ I_{\lambda_2} & = \frac{1}{2}\ln\left( I_{42} \right) = \ln \left( {\lambda_2} \right) \\ I_{\gamma} &= \frac{I _{412}}{\sqrt{I _{41} I _{42}}} = \sin\left( \gamma \right) \end{aligned} \]

\(I_{4i}=\mathbf{C}:\mathbf{L}_{ii}\) and \(I_{4ij} = \mathbf{C}:\mathbf{L}_{ij}\) and \(\mathbf{L}_{ij} = \mathbf{l}_i \otimes \mathbf{l}_j\) the structural tensor defined from the initial material warp \(\mathbf{l}_1\) and weft \(\mathbf{l}_2\) directions.

The Piola-Kirchhoff II stress tensor is given by:

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{S} &= \frac{1}{2} \frac{\partial w_{mem}}{\partial \mathbf{C}} \\ &= \frac{1}{2} \frac{\partial w_{\lambda_1}}{\partial I_{\lambda_1} } \frac{\partial I_{\lambda_1}}{\partial \mathbf{C}} + \frac{1}{2} \frac{\partial w_{\lambda_2}}{\partial I_{\lambda_2} } \frac{\partial I_{\lambda_2}}{\partial \mathbf{C}} + \frac{1}{2} \frac{\partial w_{\gamma}}{\partial I_{\gamma} } \frac{\partial I_{\gamma}}{\partial \mathbf{C}} \\ &= \mathbf{S}_{\lambda_1} + \mathbf{S}_{\lambda_2} + \mathbf{S}_{\gamma} \end{aligned} \]

Therefore, we only needs to define the strain-potential for each contribution. By default Comfor assumes that each potential can be represented by a polynomial function of the form:

\[ w_p = \sum_{i=1}^{n} {k_{i}^p (I_{p} )^{2i}} \]

Expected parameters

  • warp_ori: initial warp orientation defined by the components l1_x, l1_y, l1_z in the global base.
  • weft_ori: initial weft orientation defined by the components l2_x, l2_y, l2_z in the global base.
  • kelongwarp: warp elongation strain-potential defined by the \(n\) coefficients \(k_1^{\lambda_1},k_2^{\lambda_1} ... k_n^{\lambda_1}\).
  • kelongweft: weft elongation strain-potential defined by the \(n\) coefficients \(k_1^{\lambda_2},k_2^{\lambda_2} ... k_n^{\lambda_2}\).
  • kshear: in-plane shear strain-potential defined by the \(n\) coefficients \(k_1^{\gamma},k_2^{\gamma} ... k_n^{\gamma}\).

Example

MATERIALS TYPE HYPERTEXTILE
<material_name> RHO = <rho> DAMPING = <material_damping> WARPORI = <l1_x, l1_y, l1_z> WEFTORI = <l2_x, l2_y, l2_z> KELONGWARP = <kelong1_1, kelong1_2, kelong1_n> KELONGWEFT = <kelong2_1, kelong2_2, kelong2_n> KSHEAR = <kshear_1, kshear_2, kshear_n>

docs.title: Explicit Rayleigh Damping
docs.text: This note summarizes the mass-proportional Rayleigh damping formulation used by the explicit solver.

docs.title: Damping model
docs.text:
Comfor uses the Rayleigh model restricted to its mass-proportional part:

\[ \mathbf{C}^d = \alpha \mathbf{M} \]

where \(\alpha\) is the nodal damping coefficient.

The explicit solver advances the staggered velocity with a central-difference scheme. For a variable time step, the kick interval is:

\[ \Delta t^n = \frac{1}{2}\left(\Delta t^{n-1/2} + \Delta t^{n+1/2}\right) \]

docs.title: Damped translational update
docs.text:
At time \(t^n\), the translational equilibrium is written as:

\[ \mathbf{M}\mathbf{a}^n + \mathbf{C}^d \mathbf{v}^{n-1/2} = \mathbf{f}^n \]

Using \(\mathbf{C}^d = \alpha \mathbf{M}\) gives:

\[ \mathbf{a}^n + \alpha \mathbf{v}^{n-1/2} = \mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{f}^n \]

In Comfor, acceleration-type loads such as gravity are assembled in the physical acceleration term:

\[ \mathbf{a}_{\mathrm{phys}}^n = \mathbf{M}^{-1}\mathbf{f}^n + \mathbf{a}_{\mathrm{load}}^n \]

The damped kick is then written as:

\[ \mathbf{a}_{\mathrm{alg}}^n = \frac{\mathbf{a}_{\mathrm{phys}}^n - \alpha \mathbf{v}^{n-1/2}} {1 + \frac{1}{2}\alpha \Delta t^n} \]

The quantity stored by the solver is therefore the algorithmic acceleration used by the kick, not only the undamped physical term.

docs.title: Damped rotational update
docs.text:
The same structure is applied to rotational motion. Let \(\boldsymbol{\omega}^{n-1/2}\) be the staggered angular velocity, \(\mathbf{I}\) the nodal inertia tensor, and \(\mathbf{m}^n\) the nodal moment. The physical angular acceleration includes the gyroscopic term:

\[ \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{\mathrm{phys}}^n = \mathbf{I}^{-1}\left(\mathbf{m}^n - \boldsymbol{\omega}^{n-1/2} \times (\mathbf{I}\boldsymbol{\omega}^{n-1/2})\right) + \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{\mathrm{load}}^n \]

The damped rotational kick becomes:

\[ \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{\mathrm{alg}}^n = \frac{\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{\mathrm{phys}}^n - \alpha \boldsymbol{\omega}^{n-1/2}} {1 + \frac{1}{2}\alpha \Delta t^n} \]

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
• The formulation is consistent with the leapfrog central-difference update.
  • Translation and rotation use the same damping denominator.
  • The stored nodal accelerations are algorithmic quantities tied to the explicit update.

docs.title: Solvers Architecture in COMFOR
docs.text: COMFOR uses a modular and extensible solver architecture based on object-oriented programming principles. This section describes the current implementation and the underlying theory.

docs.text:

docs.title: ExplicitSolver: Explicit Solver Implementation
docs.text: The ExplicitSolver class is the current implementation of the explicit dynamics solver. It inherits from the Solver interface and orchestrates the resolution process.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
1. Clock management: Maintain simulation time and intervals
  2. Force assembly: Combine contributions from elements, loads, and contacts
  3. Acceleration calculation: Evaluate algorithmic acceleration for each node
  4. Integrator delegation: Hand off kinematic update to the integrator
  5. Critical time step calculation: Determine \(\Delta t_{\text{crit}}\) for the system
  6. Energy diagnostics: Update and verify energy balance

docs.title: CentralDifferenceIntegrator: Centered Differences Integrator
docs.text: The CentralDifferenceIntegrator class implements the centered differences time integration scheme for explicit dynamics.

docs.title: Algorithm
docs.text:
1. Velocity update: \(\mathbf{v}^{n+\frac{1}{2}} = \mathbf{v}^{n-\frac{1}{2}} + \Delta t^{n+\frac{1}{2}} \, \mathbf{a}^n\)
  2. Position update: \(\mathbf{u}^{n+1} = \mathbf{u}^n + \Delta t^{n+1} \, \mathbf{v}^{n+\frac{1}{2}}\)
  3. Coordinate update: \(\mathbf{x}^{n+1} = \mathbf{x}^n + \mathbf{u}^{n+1}\)

docs.title: Collaboration with ExplicitSolver
docs.text:
The integrator works in close collaboration with ExplicitSolver:

  1. ExplicitSolver assembles forces and calculates accelerations
  2. CentralDifferenceIntegrator uses these accelerations to update velocities and positions
  3. The cycle repeats for each time increment

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The scheme used in Comfor is explicit dynamics. This type of scheme allows a conditional step by step resolution of a dynamics problem. The equation of the dynamics, valid at any time, is written in the form :

For the time location of nodal quantities and the current implementation conventions used by the explicit solver, see the developer note Temporal Semantics.

\[\begin{equation} \mathbf{M} \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{C}^{d} \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{f}_{int} = \mathbf{f}_{ext} \end{equation}\]

In order to solve this equation using a time integration scheme, time is first discretized into increments, or time steps. The dynamics equation becomes :

\[\begin{equation} \mathbf{M} \mathbf{a}^i + \mathbf{C}^d \mathbf{v}^i + \mathbf{f}_{int}^i = \mathbf{f}_{ext}^i \end{equation}\]

The time integration scheme will define how displacements, velocities and accelerations are approximated from one increment to the next.

docs.title: Central difference scheme
docs.text:
The most popular, and currently implemented method on comfor is the central difference method. This method is developed from the central difference formulas applied for acceleration and velocity1 2.

Let the time of the simulation be \(t_0 \leq t \leq t_e\) be subdivided in time steps \(\Delta t^n\) from \(n=1\) to \(n = n_e\) where \(n_e\) is the number of time steps and \(t_e\) the end time of the simulation. The time after the n-th integration is \(t^n\).

\[\begin{equation} t^n = t_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{n} \Delta t^i \end{equation}\]

Without lost of generality lets put \(t_0 =0\). The coordinates of every point \(\mathbf x\) at time \(t^{n+1}\) is given by:

\[\begin{equation} \mathbf x^{n+1} = \mathbf x^{n} + \mathbf u^{n+1} \end{equation}\]

The displacement vector at time \(t+1\) are integrate using the velocities evaluated at time \(t^{n+1/2} = t^n + \frac{1}{2} \Delta t^{n+1}\)

\[ \mathbf u^{n+1} = \mathbf u^{n} + \Delta t^{n+1} \mathbf{v} \left( t_{n+1/2} \right) = \mathbf u^{n} + \Delta t^{n+1} \mathbf{v}^{n+1/2} \]

The velocity \(\mathbf{v}^{n+1/2}\) is often refereed as staggered with respect ti the coordinate system. The velocity is integrated from de from the acceleration at time \(t^n\)

\[ \mathbf{v}^{n+1/2} = \mathbf{v}^{n-1/2} + \Delta t^{n+1/2} \mathbf{a}^n \]

where \(\Delta t^{n+1/2} = \left( t^{n+1/2} - t^{n-1/2} \right)\), or:

\[ \Delta t^{n+1/2} = \frac {\Delta t^{n+1} + \Delta t^{n}}{2} \]

Finally the acceleration is obtained by solving the dynamic equilibrium at current time \(t\):

\[\begin{equation} \mathbf{a} = \mathbf{a} = \mathbf{M}^{-1}(\mathbf{f}_{ext}^n - \mathbf{f}_{int}^n - \mathbf{C}^{d}\mathbf{v}^{n-1/2} ) \end{equation}\]

This scheme as all the explicit integrations methods is conditionally stable. If the time step exceeds a critical value \(\Delta t_{crit}\) the solution will diverge. The stable time step of the dynamic system is given by:

\[ \Delta t \leq \alpha \Delta t_{crit} = \frac{2}{\omega_{max}} \]

\(\omega_{max}\) is the maximum frequency of the eigen value problem and \(\alpha\) is a safety factor, typically used to guarantee that the time step is conservative. In order to avoid a calculation of eigenvalues, this value can be bounded by taking by analogy the calculation of the eigenvalues of an elastic bar of length \(l\). The maximum frequency is given by:

\[ \omega = \frac{2}{l} \sqrt{\frac{E}{\rho}} = \frac{2c}{l} \]

The critical time step is then given by:

\[ \Delta t_{crit} = \frac{l}{c} \]

For three and three dimension, similar results apply by choosing a characteristic element length \(l_e\) and the current elastic wave speed in the element \(c_e\). During the update loop over the elements, the stable time step for each element is computed, and the minimum step time becomes the time step for the whole system.

\[ \Delta t = \alpha \min_{e} \frac{l_e}{c_e} \]

Usually a safety factor \(\alpha\) of 0.9 is used to guarantee convergence. Or, 0.25 to 0.50 in the case of problems involving explosives.

The explicit treatment of mass-proportional damping used by Comfor is described in Explicit Rayleigh Damping.

docs.title: Newmark scheme
docs.text:
The Newmark \(\beta_2\) and corresponds to a Taylor series development of the displacements, truncated at the jerk, with weighting coefficients \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\) :

\[\begin{align} \mathbf{u}^{n+1} & = \mathbf{u}^{n} + \Delta t \mathbf{v}^{n} + \frac{1}{2} \Delta t^2 \mathbf{a}^{n} + \beta \frac{1}{2} \Delta t^2 \left(\mathbf{a}^{n+1} - \mathbf{a}^{n} \right) \\ \mathbf{v}^{n+1} & = \mathbf{v}^{n} + \Delta t \mathbf{a}^{n} + \gamma \Delta t \left(\mathbf{a}^{n+1} - \mathbf{a}^{n} \right) \end{align}\]

From these expression we can write two sets, called prediction terms:

\[\begin{align} \tilde{\mathbf{u}}^{n+1} & = \mathbf{u}^{n} + \mathbf{v}^{n} + \frac{1}{2} \Delta t^2 \left( 1 - \beta \right) \mathbf{a}^{n} \\ \tilde{\mathbf{v}}^{n+1} & = \mathbf{v}^{n} + \Delta t \left( 1 - \gamma \right) \mathbf{a}^{n} \end{align}\]

and correction:

\[\begin{align} \mathbf{u}^{i+1} & = \tilde{\mathbf{u}}^{i+1} + \beta \frac{1}{2} \Delta t^2 \mathbf{a}^{i+1} \\ \mathbf{v}^{i+1} & = \tilde{\mathbf{v}}^{i+1} + \gamma \Delta t \mathbf{a}^{i+1} \end{align}\]

The objective is now to find the acceleration at the new time step:

\[ \mathbf{a}^{n+1} = - \mathbf{A}^{-1} \left( \mathbf{f}_{ext}^{n+1} + \mathbf{C}^{d} \tilde{\mathbf{v}}^{n+1} + \mathbf{K} \tilde{\mathbf{u}}^{n+1} \right) \]

where:

\[\begin{equation} \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{M} + \gamma \Delta t \mathbf{C}^{d} + \frac{1}{2} \beta \Delta t^2 \mathbf{K} \end{equation}\]

The parameters \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) of the algorithm allow to obtain different integration schemes, adapted to a given problem. Two types of resolution are then possible. The explicit resolution which allows to know the displacement at the next increment only with the help of the displacement, the speed and the acceleration at the previous step. Conversely, when this is not possible, the resolution is called implicit. The latter are generally stable for large time steps and ensure by construction the convergence of the dynamics equation. The explicit schemes are conditionally stable. Their stabilization implies the use of small time steps depending on the mesh and the material used. On the other hand, the absence of convergence verification allows to solve more easily non linear problems (geometrical, material or contact).

docs.title: Lumped mass matrix
docs.text:
In explicit dynamics, the mass and damping matrices are taken diagonally. The inversion of these matrices is then extremely simplified. A method of mass matrix condensation is used (mass lumping3). The condensation of the matrix is done by summing on the diagonal the terms of the same row:

\[\begin{equation} \tilde{M}_{ii} = \sum_j {M}_{ij} \end{equation}\]

This method using a diagonal approximation speeds up the calculation, while being reasonable since globally \(M_{ij} \neq 0\) is small for each row \(i\) and is associated with geometrically close degrees of freedom. The loss of accuracy is largely compensated by the gain in computation time. In addition, the damping matrix is computed as a function of the mass matrix using a special case of Rayleigh damping, such that \(\mathbf{C}^d=\alpha \mathbf{M}\).

docs.text:

  2. Benson, D. J. Explicit Finite Element Methods for Large Deformation Problems in Solid Mechanics. in Encyclopedia of Computational Mechanics Second Edition 1--43 (Wiley, 2017). ↩

  3. Zienkiewicz, O. C., Taylor, R. L. & Zhu, J. Z. The Finite Element Method: Its Basis and Fundamentals. (Elsevier/Butterworth-Heinemann, 2005). ↩

What are the system requirements for Comfor?

Comfor is supported on Windows (win64), Linux (amd64), and macOS (amd64). Using any other architecture is not guaranteed to work. Minimum requirements:

comfor <input_file_name>

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: This tool has been compiled and tested on Windows (x86_64, ARM64), Linux (x86_64, ARM64), and macOS (x86_64, Apple Silicon). Using any other architecture is not guaranteed to work.

docs.title: Download
docs.text:
To run COMFOR, you can download the binaries from the release page or you can build it from source. Download the binary for your architecture, follow the instructions given here, and run some tests.

To build COMFOR from sources, you will need to download and compile the code. If so, follow the instructions below.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
CMake: A cross-platform, open-source build system generator. It allows you to generate a project for a given IDE (Unix Makefiles, Xcode, Visual Studio, etc.) or compilation rules for COMFOR. It can be easily installed under Linux with the following command:

sudo apt install cmake

On macOS using brew:

brew install cmake

Binary files for macOS and Windows can be downloaded at cmake.org.

C++ Compiler

COMFOR is written in C++ and requires a C++ compiler that supports C++17 features or higher.

Recommended versions:

  • GCC >= 11
  • Clang >= 14
  • Apple Clang >= 13.0.0
  • MSVC >= 2022

Under Ubuntu 22.04 / 24.04 LTS, you can install the necessary tools with:

sudo apt install build-essential

Under macOS, verify if the Clang compiler is already installed:

clang --version

To install or update the Clang compilers, enter:

command xcode-select --install

Under Windows, you can use a POSIX environment like MSYS2 or MinGW-w64. COMFOR is also fully compatible with Microsoft C++ compilers (Tested using Visual Studio 2022).

Warning

Some versions of MinGW may have compatibility issues with google-test (see issue 2418). While you can compile COMFOR, building the unit tests might require specific configurations.

Python

Note

Python is mainly used for result post-processing, automated testing, and generating this documentation.

Make sure Python 3.10+ and the following packages are installed:

  • Charts: Matplotlib
  • Documentation: MkDocs-Material

Install the packages using pip:

python3 -m pip install matplotlib mkdocs-material

Warning

On Windows, it is recommended to use the standalone Python.org distribution. Ensure that python and pip are added to your system PATH.

docs.title: Clone
docs.text:
Clone or download the sources from the main repo.

git clone https://gitlab.com/comfor/comfor.git

docs.title: Using CMake (Recommended)
docs.text:
The compilation rules are generated by CMake using the CMakeLists.txt file included in the project. A good habit is to encapsulate all intermediate files in a single folder (the build). CMake identifies the architecture and generates the project rules.

cd COMFOR
mkdir build
cd build
cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release ..
cmake --build . --config Release

The executable comfor is located in the bin folder of the build directory (bin/Release with multi-configuration generators such as Visual Studio).

Tip

CMake can generate projects for different IDEs (Visual Studio, Xcode, Eclipse). You can specify a generator using cmake .. -G <generator_name>. To see the available list for your system, use cmake -G.

docs.title: Cross-platform proposition
docs.text: If you prefer a graphical interface, you can use Visual Studio Code with the "C/C++" and "CMake Tools" extensions to automate the compilation process.

docs.title: Execution Options (CLI)
docs.text: COMFOR is a command-line tool. You can control its behavior using various arguments to manage parallel execution, validate files, or display software information.

docs.title: Available Arguments
docs.text: Argument Long Form Value Description -j --job FILE Required. Path to the input file (.toml, or .txt/.in for the legacy Fembic format). -o --output PATH Result root directory (default: Results_<input_name>/ next to the input file). - --validate - Validates the input file without running the solver. -u --cpus 1 Number of CPUs. The current build is serial: only 1 is accepted (default). -i --info - Shows general information about COMFOR. -c --credits - Lists software contributors and libraries. -l --license - Displays the software license terms. -v --version - Shows the current version. -h --help - Prints the help message.

docs.title: Run and test
docs.text: You should now have an executable file called COMFOR (or comfor.exe on Windows).

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
To launch a simulation, navigate to your work directory and use the -j (or --job) flag followed by your input file.

# Standard execution
./comfor -j Examples/input_file.toml

# Write the results in a custom directory
./comfor -j Examples/input_file.toml -o run-01

Tip

The -j argument is required. See Running the Analysis for all the options and the generated files.

docs.title: Validate it
docs.text:
If you want to check your input file for syntax errors or missing parameters without starting the actual computation, use the --validate flag:

./comfor -j Examples/input_file.toml --validate

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
When the project is configured with -DCOMFOR_TEST=ON, CMake also generates a series of test executables (e.g., AmplitudeTest, MaterialTest). These allow you to verify if the different COMFOR modules are working correctly on your machine.

Example:

./AmplitudeTest

Expected result:

[==========] Running 5 tests from 1 test suite.
[----------] Global test environment set-up.
[----------] 5 tests from TabularTest
[ RUN      ] TabularTest.parseOne
[       OK ] TabularTest.parseOne (0 ms)
...
[  PASSED  ] 5 tests.

docs.title: Postprocessing
docs.text: COMFOR generates VTU or VTK files for the results. ParaView is the recommended open-source post-processor to visualize these results. ParaView is available at paraview.org.

docs.title: Complete Tutorial: Double Dome Benchmark
docs.text: This tutorial guides you step-by-step through creating and running a Double Dome simulation with COMFOR. The Double Dome benchmark is a standard test in the composite forming community, used to evaluate the ability of simulation codes to model the forming of complex composite structures.

docs.title: Introduction to the Double Dome Benchmark
What is the Double Dome?
docs.text:
The Double Dome is a widely used numerical benchmark in the field of composite material forming simulation. It consists of a flat plate being formed into a double dome shape by a central punch. This test evaluates:

  • The code's ability to handle large deformations
  • The accuracy of composite material behavior modeling
  • Contact management between punch, die, and plate
  • Numerical stability for explicit simulations

docs.title: Benchmark Configuration
docs.text: Parameter Value Material Textile composite (HYPERTEXTILE) Plate thickness 1.0 mm Punch speed 10 mm/s (reached after a 1 s ramp) Punch stroke 65 mm Simulation duration 7 seconds Friction Coulomb coefficient = 0.1

docs.title: Geometry
docs.text:
• Plate: Flat textile sheet, meshed with 3-node triangles
  • Punch: Double-dome shaped rigid tool
  • Die: Matching rigid cavity

docs.title: Required Files
docs.text: To follow this tutorial, you will need the mesh files:

docs.title: Available Meshes
docs.text: COMFOR provides two versions of the benchmark:

docs.title: 1. Full Model
docs.text:
• Complete geometry, without symmetry
  • Contains: die.inp, plate.inp, punch.inp
  • Download: full/die.inp, full/plate.inp, full/punch.inp

docs.title: 2. Quarter Model (Recommended for tutorial)
docs.text:
• Faster simulations exploiting the double symmetry of the benchmark
  • Contains: die.inp, plate.inp, punch.inp, plate.msh
  • Size: 1 892 nodes and 3 492 elements once the three parts are assembled
  • Download: quart/die.inp, quart/plate.inp, quart/plate.msh, quart/punch.inp

Recommendation

For this tutorial, we use the quarter model which is faster to run while demonstrating all features.

docs.title: Step 1: Understanding the TOML File Structure
docs.text: The double-dome.toml file is structured into multiple blocks that define the complete simulation. Let's examine each section:

docs.title: Global Structure
docs.text:
double-dome.toml
├── [model]          # Simulation metadata (informative)
├── [control]        # Time parameters
├── [output.*]       # Output configuration (1)
├── [mesh.*]         # Mesh sources (3)
├── [part.*]         # Physical components (3)
├── [set.*]          # Entity groups (5)
├── [material.*]     # Constitutive laws (1)
├── [section.*]      # Physical properties (2)
├── [[section_assignments]] # Associations (3)
├── [amplitude.*]    # Time functions (1)
├── [constraint.*]   # Boundary conditions (4)
├── [contact_behaviour.*] # Contact laws (2)
└── [contact.*]      # Contact definition (1)

docs.title: Step 2: Create the Input File
docs.text: Create a file double-dome.toml with the following content. We will explain each section in detail.

docs.title: Section 1: Model Metadata
docs.text:
# --- Model ---
[model]
name = "Double-dome"
author = "Innovamics"
date = "2026-08-05"
description = "Double-dome Benchmark"

This block is optional and purely informative: it documents the model but is not used by the solver.

docs.title: Section 2: Simulation Control
docs.text:
# --- Control ---
[control]
run_from = 0.0
run_to = 7.0
  • run_from: Start time (usually 0.0)
  • run_to: End time of simulation (7 seconds for the full punch stroke)

Time Step

The time step is not specified here. COMFOR automatically calculates it based on mesh and material properties.

docs.title: Section 3: Output Configuration
docs.text:
# --- Output ---
[output.vtus]
type = "VTU"
frequency = 0.1
format = "BINARY"
Parameter Value Description vtus (name) Name of the output, given by the table header [output.vtus]. Also used as the name of the result sub-folder and files type "VTU" Output format (recommended) frequency 0.1 Write results every 0.1 seconds format "BINARY" Binary format for smaller files

Output Directory

By default, results are written to Results_double-dome/, next to the input file. The frames of this output are stored in Results_double-dome/vtus/.

docs.title: Section 4: Mesh Import
docs.text:
# --- Mesh import ---
[mesh.punch]
type = "ABAQUS"
file = "quart/punch.inp"

[mesh.die]
type = "ABAQUS"
file = "quart/die.inp"

[mesh.plate]
type = "GMSH"
file = "quart/plate.msh"

Explanations: - punch: Hemispherical punch (Abaqus .inp format) - die: Die/cavity (Abaqus .inp format) - plate: Plate to be formed (Gmsh .msh format)

File Paths

Relative mesh paths are resolved from the directory containing the TOML file. Make sure the mesh files are in a quart/ directory next to double-dome.toml, or adjust the paths accordingly.

docs.title: Section 5: Part Definitions
docs.text:
# --- Parts ---
[part.punch]
mesh = "punch"
element_mapping = { "S3" = "CONTACT_TRIANGLE" }
translation = [-1.0, -1.0, 10.0]

[part.die]
mesh = "die"
element_mapping = { "S3" = "CONTACT_TRIANGLE" }
translation = [-1.0, -1.0, 0.0]

[part.plate]
mesh = "plate"
element_mapping = { "2" = "DKT18" }
translation = [0.0, 0.0, 1.0]

Explanations:

Part Mesh Mapping Translation Role punch punch S3 → CONTACT_TRIANGLE [-1, -1, 10] Movable punch die die S3 → CONTACT_TRIANGLE [-1, -1, 0] Fixed die plate plate 2 → DKT18 [0, 0, 1] Plate to form

Element Mapping

The keys of element_mapping are the element types as written in the mesh file:

  • Abaqus S3 triangles (read as S3L_C0 by default) are mapped to CONTACT_TRIANGLE for the punch and the die (rigid contact surfaces).
  • Gmsh triangles (type 2, read as MEMBRANE_3 by default) are mapped to DKT18 for the plate (shell triangle with bending).

See the Mesh block for the full translation tables.

Translation

Translations are used to position parts in space. The punch starts above the plate (z=10.0), the plate at z=1.0 and the die below (z=0.0).

docs.title: Section 6: Set Definitions (Groups)
docs.text:
# --- Sets ---
[set.punchNodes]
type = "NODE"
part = "punch"

[set.punchElements]
type = "ELEMENT"
part = "punch"

[set.dieNodes]
type = "NODE"
part = "die"

[set.dieElements]
type = "ELEMENT"
part = "die"

[set.plateElements]
type = "ELEMENT"
part = "plate"

[set.plateXNodes]
type = "NODE"
part = "plate"
range = [1, 666, 35]

[set.plateYNodes]
type = "NODE"
part = "plate"
range = [1, 35, 1]

Explanations:

Set Type Part Selection Usage punchNodes NODE punch All nodes Velocity constraint punchElements ELEMENT punch All elements Section assignment dieNodes NODE die All nodes Fixed constraint dieElements ELEMENT die All elements Section assignment plateElements ELEMENT plate All elements Section assignment plateXNodes NODE plate Nodes 1, 36, 71,... X constraint plateYNodes NODE plate Nodes 1-35 Y constraint

Range Selection

  • range = [1, 666, 35]: Selects nodes 1, 36, 71, 106, ... 666 (increment of 35)
  • range = [1, 35, 1]: Selects nodes 1 to 35 (increment of 1)

docs.title: Section 7: Materials
docs.text:
# --- Materials ---
[material.HyperTex]
type = "HYPERTEXTILE"
density = 1e-6
damping = 5.0
warp_orientation = [1.0, 0.0, 0.0]
weft_orientation = [0.0, 1.0, 0.0]
k_elong_warp = [100.0]
k_elong_weft = [100.0]
k_shear = [0.0185, 0.0464, -0.0213]
k_bend_warp = [5.0]
k_bend_weft = [5.0]
k_bend_twist = [0.0]

Composite Material Properties:

Parameter Value Description type "HYPERTEXTILE" Composite material model density 1e-6 Mass density (ton/mm³) damping 5.0 Rayleigh damping warp_orientation [1,0,0] Warp fiber direction weft_orientation [0,1,0] Weft fiber direction k_elong_warp [100.0] Tensile stiffness (warp) k_elong_weft [100.0] Tensile stiffness (weft) k_shear [0.0185, 0.0464, -0.0213] Shear stiffness k_bend_warp [5.0] Bending stiffness (warp) k_bend_weft [5.0] Bending stiffness (weft) k_bend_twist [0.0] Twist stiffness

docs.title: Section 8: Sections
docs.text:
# --- Sections ---
[section.toolSection]
type = "RIGID"
thickness = 2.0

[section.plateSection]
type = "SHELL_GENERALIZED"
material = "HyperTex"
thickness = 1.0

[[section_assignments]]
name = "AssignPunch"
section = "toolSection"
set = "punchElements"

[[section_assignments]]
name = "AssignDie"
section = "toolSection"
set = "dieElements"

[[section_assignments]]
name = "AssignPlate"
section = "plateSection"
set = "plateElements"

Explanations:

Section Type Material Thickness Usage toolSection RIGID - 2.0 mm For punch and die (rigid bodies) plateSection SHELL_GENERALIZED HyperTex 1.0 mm For deformable plate

Assignments: - Punch uses toolSection (rigid) - Die uses toolSection (rigid) - Plate uses plateSection (deformable composite)

docs.title: Section 9: Amplitudes
docs.text:
# --- Amplitudes ---
[amplitude.punchAmplitude]
type = "TABULAR"
values = [[0.0, 0.0],
          [1.0, 1.0],
          [10.0, 1.0]]

Explanations: - type = "TABULAR": Function defined by points - values: [time, value] pairs - At t=0.0s: value = 0.0 (start from rest) - At t=1.0s: value = 1.0 (full speed) - At t=10.0s: value = 1.0 (speed maintained)

This amplitude is used to modulate the punch velocity.

docs.title: Section 10: Constraints (Boundary Conditions)
docs.text:
# --- constraints ---
[constraint.fixX]
type = "BOUNDARY_CONDITION"
set = "plateXNodes"
vx = 0.0

[constraint.fixY]
type = "BOUNDARY_CONDITION"
set = "plateYNodes"
vy = 0.0
vrx = 0.0

[constraint.fixPunch]
type = "BOUNDARY_CONDITION"
set = "punchNodes"
vx = 0.0
vy = 0.0
vz = {value = -10.0, amplitude = "punchAmplitude" }

[constraint.fixDie]
type = "BOUNDARY_CONDITION"
set = "dieNodes"
preset = "FIXED"

Explanations:

Constraint Set DOFs Value fixX plateXNodes vx 0.0 (blocked in X) fixY plateYNodes vy, vrx 0.0 (blocked in Y and rotation X) fixPunch punchNodes vx, vy 0.0 (laterally blocked) fixPunch punchNodes vz -10.0 with amplitude (downward speed) fixDie dieNodes all FIXED (completely fixed)

FIXED Preset

The "FIXED" preset blocks all degrees of freedom (vx, vy, vz, vrx, vry, vrz).

Punch Speed

The punch moves downward at 10 mm/s (negative = downward), modulated by the amplitude which ramps from 0 to 1 during the first second. Over 7 s the punch therefore travels 0.5 × 10 × 1 + 10 × 6 = 65 mm.

docs.title: Section 11: Contact Behaviors
docs.text:
# --- Contact Behaviors ---
[contact_behaviour.PENALTY_GENERAL]
type = "LINEAR_PENALTY"
stiffness = 10.0

[contact_behaviour.COULOMB_GENERAL]
type = "COULOMB"
friction = 0.1

Explanations:

Behavior Type Parameter Value PENALTY_GENERAL LINEAR_PENALTY stiffness 10.0 (penalty stiffness) COULOMB_GENERAL COULOMB friction 0.1 (friction coefficient)

docs.title: Section 12: Contact
docs.text:
# --- Contacts (General) ---
[contact.GENERAL_CONTACT]
type = "GENERAL"
normal = "PENALTY_GENERAL"
tangential = "COULOMB_GENERAL"

Explanations: - type = "GENERAL": General contact between all surfaces - normal = "PENALTY_GENERAL": Normal contact law (penalty) - tangential = "COULOMB_GENERAL": Tangential contact law (Coulomb friction)

General Contact

General contact does not require explicit surface definitions: interactions are detected over the whole model. Only one GENERAL contact can be defined per model.

docs.title: Step 3: Validate the File
docs.text:
Before running the simulation, it is highly recommended to validate the input file:

comfor -j double-dome.toml --validate

Expected Output (after the banner):

 Logging job double-dome
 =======================================
 File info
  > File name: double-dome.toml
  > Extension: .toml
 Parse validation
  > Validation successful. No errors found.
 Exit Comfor

The same information is written to double-dome.md, next to the input file. When errors are found, all of them are listed in this file under Validation Errors.

Scope of the validation

--validate checks the syntax, the mandatory parameters, the allowed values and the uniqueness of names. Some checks require the model to be built (e.g. element/section compatibility, which depends on element_mapping); they are performed when the simulation starts.

Fixing Errors

If errors are reported:

  1. Check that all mesh file paths are correct
  2. Check that all references exist (e.g., material.HyperTex is referenced in section.plateSection)
  3. Check that every block that requires it has a name (e.g. [output.vtus], or name = ... inside [[output]] and [[section_assignments]])

docs.title: Step 4: Run the Simulation
docs.text:
Once validation is successful, run the simulation:

comfor -j double-dome.toml

Options:

  • -j double-dome.toml: Specify the input file (required)
  • -o <path>: Optional, write the results to another directory (see Running the Analysis)

Output during execution (extract):

 Model info
  > Number of objects instances
   - Nodes: 1892
   - Elements: 3492
   ...
  > Automatic step time: true
   - Step time: 0.000446
 Running info
 =======================================
  > Writing output file 1
   - Elapsed time: 0.395195
   - Current time: 0.100326
   - Time step: 0.000446
   - Internal energy: 0.000000
   - Kinetic energy: 0.000000
   - Ek/Ei (%): ...
 =======================================
 ...
 =======================================
  > Writing output file 70
   - Elapsed time: 34.176837
   - Current time: 7.000105
   - Time step: 0.000273
   - Internal energy: 77.677680
   - Kinetic energy: 5.454920
   - Ek/Ei (%): 7.022506
 =======================================
 Solving took : 34.225519
 Exit Comfor

A block is printed each time an output frame is written (every 0.1 s here). At the end of the forming, the kinetic energy is about 7 % of the internal energy: the simulation remains quasi-static. The time step is computed automatically and may decrease during the forming as elements distort.

Execution Time

With the quarter model, the simulation takes about 30 seconds on a recent laptop (serial execution).

Existing results

The results directory must not exist before the run. To run the same file again, delete Results_double-dome/ or use -o to choose another directory.

docs.title: Results Structure
docs.text:
After execution, the following files are available:

double-dome.toml
double-dome.md                  # Job log
Results_double-dome/
├── manifest.toml               # Run status and list of generated files
└── vtus/                       # One folder per output (its name)
    ├── vtus_000000.vtu
    ├── vtus_000001.vtu
    │   ... (1 file every 0.1 seconds)
    └── vtus_000070.vtu

docs.title: Visualization with ParaView
docs.text:
1. Launch ParaView
  2. Open files: Select the vtus_..vtu group in Results_double-dome/vtus/
  3. Apply: Click the Apply button to display the mesh

docs.title: Deformation Visualization
docs.text:
• The mesh is written at its current position: the displayed geometry is already the deformed one
  • Color it with Displacement (magnitude or Z component)
  • Use the VCR toolbar to play the animation
Deformed plate at end of simulation

docs.title: Fabric Visualization
docs.text:
• Select ShearAngle to see the in-plane shear of the fabric (the key result of the double-dome benchmark)
  • Select FiberStress or FiberStrain (2 components: warp and weft) to see the fiber tension
  • FiberOrientationWarp / FiberOrientationWeft show the current fiber directions (e.g. with the Glyph filter)
  • Adjust color scale to see the distribution

docs.title: Part Selection
docs.text:
• Apply a Threshold filter on PartID to display only the plate (the tools hide it at the end of the forming). Here PartID is 0 for the die, 1 for the plate and 2 for the punch
  • The rigid tools have no stress or strain: their cell values are NaN, which ParaView displays with the NaN color

docs.title: Tracker Analysis
docs.text: If you add trackers (not included in this basic example), one CSV file per tracker is written in Results_double-dome/ (e.g. Results_double-dome/PunchForce.csv). See Trackers.

docs.title: Simulation Verification
docs.text:
1. Run status: Results_double-dome/manifest.toml must contain status = 'completed'
  2. Energies: In a quasi-static forming simulation, the kinetic energy should stay small compared to the internal energy. Monitor the Ek/Ei (%) ratio printed at each output
  3. Time step: Should remain stable (no drastic reduction)

docs.title: Common Issues
docs.text: Issue Cause Solution Directory already exists Results from a previous run Delete the results directory or use -o assigned section must be of type ... Element type and section do not match Check element_mapping (keys = types of the mesh file) and section_assignments High Ek/Ei (%) Dynamic effects too large Reduce the punch speed or increase damping Slow simulation Mesh too fine or small time step Use the quarter model or coarsen the mesh Punch penetration Insufficient contact stiffness Increase stiffness in PENALTY_GENERAL

docs.title: Complete File
docs.text: You can download the complete file here: double-dome.toml

docs.title: Exercise: Customize the Simulation
docs.text:
Try modifying the following parameters and observe the differences:

  1. Punch speed: Change vz = -10.0 to -5.0 or -20.0
  2. Amplitude: Modify punchAmplitude for progressive acceleration
  3. Friction: Change friction = 0.1 to 0.0 or 0.2
  4. Material stiffness: Modify k_elong_warp and k_elong_weft
  5. Plate thickness: Change thickness = 1.0 to 0.5 or 2.0

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
You have now: - ✅ Understood the Double Dome benchmark - ✅ Created a complete TOML input file - ✅ Imported external meshes (Abaqus, Gmsh) - ✅ Defined composite materials - ✅ Configured contact with friction - ✅ Run an explicit simulation - ✅ Visualized results with ParaView

The Double Dome benchmark is a well-established test case in the composite forming community, widely used for validation and comparison of numerical simulation codes 1 2 3.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Try with the full model (full/*.inp); note that the full punch uses Abaqus R3D3 elements, mapped with element_mapping = { "R3D3" = "CONTACT_TRIANGLE" }
  • Add trackers to record punch force
  • Modify geometry to create a new benchmark
  • Try with different material types (ELASTIC, etc.)
  • Explore other examples in the documentation

docs.title: Services
docs.text: Through the Comfor Academy, we provide dedicated training programs for students, researchers, and academic institutions. Our goal is to make advanced simulation techniques for composite forming and processing accessible to learners of all levels, helping them gain confidence, efficiency, and save valuable time in their thesis or research preparation.

docs.title: Training Programs
docs.text:
Our academic training is focused on bridging theory and practice in numerical simulation.

We offer:

  • Simulation with Comfor: hands-on sessions to learn, use, and master the Comfor environment for material forming and contact mechanics
  • Scientific software development: courses coveqring the fundamentals and best practices of modern C++ and Python development applied to simulation and research workflows

These programs help students and educators build strong technical foundations, develop research autonomy, and apply simulation tools effectively to real engineering or scientific challenges.

docs.title: Collaboration
docs.text:
We actively collaborate with universities, research laboratories, and academic partners on research and development projects. Our aim is to accelerate innovation and promote open, reproducible science in the field of composites simulation.

Together, we can:

  • Develop and validate new simulation techniques
  • Propose and implement advanced constitutive models
  • Co-supervise academic theses and research projects

If your institution is seeking an academic or industrial partner in simulation and modeling, we are ready to work with you.

docs.title: Comfor Editions
docs.text:
Comfor is distributed under a dual licensing model to support both open research and industrial applications.

  • Comfor Community (Open Source): Open-source edition for research and education, enabling transparency, reproducibility, and collaborative innovation.
  • Comfor Enterprise (Commercial License): Professional edition designed and maintained by Innovamics, offering enhanced performance, stability, and dedicated support.
